parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman phones a company to hire a van for moving house.
script: Good afternoon, Easy Move Van Hire. This is Paul. How can I help you?
Hello. I'm moving flat next month and I'd like to hire a van for a day.
No problem. Which date are you thinking of?
Let me check. Yes, we have vans available on the 14th. How much are you moving? Is it a whole house or a few items?
It's a one-bedroom flat. A bed, a sofa, a small table and about twenty boxes.
Then I'd suggest our medium van. The small van is really only for a few pieces of furniture. The medium one is 72 pounds for the day, and the large is 95.
The medium sounds right. Does that include insurance?
Basic insurance is included. If you want to reduce the amount you pay if there's any damage, you can add extra cover for 12 pounds a day.
I'll take the extra cover, thanks. I'm not used to driving big vehicles.
Very sensible. Now, do you need any equipment? We hire out a trolley for moving heavy items, and moving blankets to protect furniture.
Just the blankets, please. A friend is lending me a trolley.
Fine. Blankets are 2 pounds each. How many would you like?
Six blankets. Now I just need a few details. Your full name?
Thank you. And a contact number?
And you'll need to bring your driving licence when you collect the van, and a credit card for the deposit. The deposit is 150 pounds, which we return when the van comes back undamaged.
Can I pay the deposit with a debit card?
I'm afraid it has to be a credit card.
OK. Where do I collect the van?
Our depot is on Canal Street, number 18, behind the large supermarket. We open at 7.30 on Saturdays.
And what time does it have to be back?
By 6 pm the same day. If you're late, there's a charge of 10 pounds per hour.
That's clear. Thank you very much.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: An organiser gives information about a weekend food festival.
script: Hello everyone, and thanks for coming to this briefing about the Harbourside Food Festival, which takes place on the last weekend of this month. I'll give you the key information and then explain the layout of the site.

This is our fifth festival. In the first year we had around forty stalls; this year there will be over a hundred, mostly small local producers. The big change this year is that the festival is completely cashless, so please remind visitors that they'll need a card or phone to pay. There is no entry fee on Saturday or Sunday, although the cookery demonstrations need to be booked in advance online, because places are limited.

We've had a lot of questions about transport. The car park next to the harbour will be closed all weekend, because that's where some of the stalls will be. Instead, there's a free shuttle bus from the railway station every fifteen minutes. Visitors who come by bike can leave it at the bike park near the north gate.
We are also trying hard to reduce waste. All stallholders must use compostable plates and cutlery, and visitors who bring their own cup will get fifty pence off any hot drink.

Now, the layout. If you come in through the main gate on Harbour Road, the information tent is immediately on your right. Straight ahead, in the centre of the site, is the main stage, where we have live music both days. To the left of the main stage, along the water, you'll find the seafood stalls, which are always the busiest. The cookery demonstration tent is behind the main stage, at the far end of the site.

Families should head to the children's area, which is next to the north gate, so it's well away from the road. And the first aid point is beside the information tent, so it's easy to find. Finally, the toilets are at the east end of the site, opposite the seafood stalls.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two trainee nurses, Priya and Ben, discuss a group assignment about sleep with their supervisor.
script: So, Priya, Ben, you've chosen sleep among night-shift workers for your assignment. Why that topic?

Partly because we both started night shifts last month. But mainly because we noticed how little advice the hospital gives new staff about it. There's lots of information about patient safety, but almost nothing about looking after yourself.
That's a good reason. What have you found so far?

We've read about twenty studies. The thing that stood out for me was that most night workers don't actually sleep less in total, but their sleep is broken into shorter pieces, and that seems to be what makes them tired.
I was more surprised by the research on light. Even ten minutes of bright light on the journey home in the morning makes it much harder to fall asleep.
Wearing sunglasses on the way home is an easy one. And we'll recommend a short nap before the first night shift, rather than trying to stay awake all day.
And are you planning to collect any data of your own?

We wanted to give a questionnaire to all the nurses on our ward, but the ethics committee would take two months to approve it, which is too long. So instead we'll do short interviews with five experienced nurses, which our ward manager says is fine as long as we don't record names.
That's sensible. Now, how will you divide the work? The deadline is in three weeks.
I'll do the interviews, because I'm on day shifts next week, so it's easier to find people.
And I'll write the literature review, since I've read most of the articles on light.
Who's preparing the leaflet for new staff? That's part of the assessment.
We'll do that together, because it should combine both parts.
And Ben's going to check the references. He's much more careful than me.
What about the presentation to the team?
I'll give that. Ben will be on nights by then.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A talk about the history and future of honeybees in cities.
script: In today's talk I want to look at a trend that surprises many people: the growth of beekeeping in cities.

Keeping bees is nothing new. Records from ancient Egypt show bees being kept in clay pots, and honey was so valuable that it was sometimes used to pay taxes. For most of history, however, beekeeping was a rural activity.

That has changed dramatically in the last twenty years. In London alone, the number of registered hives roughly doubled in a decade. Hives can now be found on the roofs of hotels, offices and even museums.

Why do bees do well in cities? One reason is variety. Parks and private gardens contain a huge range of flowering plants, so city bees have food for a longer season than bees in the countryside, where large farms often grow a single crop. Another reason is that cities use fewer pesticides than intensive agriculture.

However, there is a problem. Honeybees are only one of around two hundred and fifty species of bee in Britain, and most of the others are wild, solitary bees. When too many hives are placed in one area, honeybees compete with these wild species for the same flowers. Some scientists now argue that the number of hives in central London has grown beyond what the available flowers can support.

So what should cities do? Rather than adding more hives, experts recommend planting more flowers, especially native species that bloom early and late in the year. Leaving areas of grass uncut also helps, because many wild bees nest in the ground. And some councils have started to build what they call bee hotels, which are simple wooden structures with holes where solitary bees can lay their eggs.

Finally, a word about honey. City honey is often described as having a more complex flavour than country honey, simply because the bees visit so many different plants. Tests have also shown that it contains very low levels of pollution, which reassures many buyers.

B  Family Stream. Up to 150 Mbps, enough for several people streaming films at the same time. £34 a month, 18-month contract. Includes a free subscription to a TV streaming service for the first six months.

To check whether your item has been found, complete the online form, giving as much detail as possible. We will contact you by email if we find a match. Please do not phone the office, as staff are unable to check items over the phone.

If you cannot come in person, we can post most items to you for an additional fee. Bicycles and large items such as suitcases cannot be posted.

paras: Every permanent employee has an annual training budget of £800, which can be used for courses, conferences or professional exams. Part-time staff receive a budget in proportion to their hours.

passages.title: Why do we keep pets?
paras: A  Around half of all households in many Western countries include at least one pet, and spending on animals has grown steadily for decades. At first sight this is puzzling. Pets cost money and time, they rarely provide anything that people need to survive, and caring for them can limit where owners live and travel. Biologists have long asked why a species would put so much effort into looking after animals that are not its own young.

B  One explanation is practical. For thousands of years, dogs helped people to hunt and to guard their homes, and cats kept stores of grain free from mice. On this view, the modern pet is simply a working animal that has lost its job. Yet this cannot explain why people keep goldfish, rabbits or parrots, which have never had any useful function in most societies.

C  A second theory points to health. Several studies in the 1980s and 1990s reported that pet owners had lower blood pressure and visited the doctor less often. These findings were widely reported in newspapers. More recent and larger studies, however, have produced mixed results. Psychologist Dr Hannah Moore notes that people who are already healthy and active may be more likely to get a dog in the first place. 'Owning a dog may not make you healthy,' she says. 'It may be that healthy people choose dogs.'

D  A third explanation focuses on our attraction to faces. Many popular pets, such as cats and some breeds of dog, have large eyes, round heads and small noses, features that resemble those of human babies. According to this theory, people care for pets because the animals trigger the same instincts that make us protect our own children. Critics point out, though, that many people keep snakes or spiders, which have none of these features.

E  Perhaps the most convincing idea is that pet keeping is a cultural habit that spreads from person to person. Anthropologist James Serpell has shown that the kind of pet people keep, and whether they keep one at all, varies greatly between societies and over time. Children who grow up with animals are much more likely to keep pets as adults, and fashions for particular breeds rise and fall much as fashions in clothes do.

F  None of these theories is complete on its own, and most researchers now accept that people keep animals for a mixture of reasons. What is clear is that pets matter to their owners: in surveys, a large majority of owners describe their pet as a member of the family.
